_comment: Elbe-Slav (Polabian) deities and temples cut from Machal, Slavic Mythology (Mythology of All Races III, 1918), Part II. All passages paraphrase.

title.en: Procopius' Testimony: The One God Who Makes the Lightning
title.zh: 普羅科匹厄斯所證：造雷電之獨一神

region.en: Lower Danube, lands of the early Slavs (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 多瑙河下游早期斯拉夫人之地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Written c. 545 CE (Procopius, Gothic War III.14); recorded by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II intro, quoting Procopius, De Bello Gothico iii.14

summary.en: The oldest external witness to Slavic religion: Procopius reports that the Slavs and Antae believe in one single god, the creator of lightning and lord of all things, to whom they sacrifice cattle — while rivers, nymphs, and other beings receive offerings and oracles beside him.
summary.zh: 斯拉夫宗教最古之外證：普羅科匹厄斯記斯拉夫人與安特人信獨一神——雷電之造者、萬物之主，宰牲祭之；河流、仙靈等亦受祭並示神諭。

sensitivity.note: Byzantine literary source; no living community.

passages.text: Procopius, the Greek historian of the sixth century, writes of the Slavs and Antae: 'They believe that there is one single god who is the creator of the lightning and the sole lord of all things, and to him they sacrifice cattle and all sorts of animals.' Beside this supreme thunder-lord they worship rivers, nymphs, and other deities, sacrificing to all and divining the future from the offerings.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II intro, quoting Procopius; not verbatim.

passages.text: Helmold, chronicling the Elbe Slavs six centuries later, preserves the same shape of belief: among the multiform divine powers who rule fields, forests, sorrows, and joys, one god rules over the others in heaven, pre-eminent in might and caring only for things celestial, while the rest obey the duties assigned them, sprung from his blood and honoured in proportion to their nearness to that god of gods. The name of the chief god has not come down to us, though belief identifies him with Svarog, the heavenly smith.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II intro, quoting Helmold; not verbatim.

title.en: The Harvest Festival of Svantovit at Arkona
title.zh: 阿科納的斯萬托維特豐收祭

region.en: Arkona, isle of Rugen (symbolic pin at Cape Arkona)
region.zh: 呂根島阿科納（象徵性定位於阿科納角）

texts.period: Recorded by Saxo Grammaticus c. 1200 (rite pre-1168); recorded by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 1, after Saxo Grammaticus

summary.en: After harvest all Rugen gathers at Arkona: the priest, holding his breath to keep from defiling the god's presence, reads the coming year in the mead sunk in the great horn; a man-sized honey cake is held up with the question 'Can you see me?' — and the wish not to see him next year promises a better harvest.
summary.zh: 豐收之後全島聚於阿科納：祭司屏息以免褻瀆神前，觀蜜酒之降以卜來歲；舉人形蜜糕問『可見我否』——祈來年不見，即兆豐年。

sensitivity.note: Historical rite; the 'see me' formula survives in Slavic Christmas and All-Souls customs.

passages.text: Shortly after harvest a great festival was held in honour of Svantovit, and people assembled from all quarters of the island of Rugen to sacrifice cattle and join the rites. The day before, the sanctuary was carefully swept by the priest, who alone had access to it; while he remained inside he was careful not to breathe, and when he could no longer hold his breath he hastened to the door, lest the presence of the deity be desecrated by the exhalation of a mortal man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 1, after Saxo; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the following day, while the people waited before the entrance, the priest took the great horn from the god's hands: if the mead had sunk, a bad harvest was foretold and the hearers were advised to reserve grain against dearth. He poured the old wine at the divinity's feet, refilled the horn, and asked for victory and increase; then, at one draught, he emptied the cup himself and placed it again in the god's right hand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 1; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then a festal cake as large as a man, flavoured with honey, was brought in. Placing it between himself and the people the priest asked whether he was visible to them, and on their answering yes, expressed the wish that they might not see him next year — a ceremony believed to ensure a better harvest. He admonished them to keep dutiful homage to the god, and the rest of the day was given to carousing, it being accounted a proof of piety to be drunk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 1; not verbatim.

title.en: The White Horse of Svantovit: Divination by Spear-Fence
title.zh: 斯萬托維特之白馬：矛柵占卜

region.en: Arkona, isle of Rugen (symbolic pin at Cape Arkona)
region.zh: 呂根島阿科納（象徵性定位於阿科納角）

texts.period: Recorded by Saxo Grammaticus c. 1200; recorded by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 1

summary.en: A sacred white horse is kept for Svantovit, groomed by the high priest, found sweating at dawn from the god's midnight rides; before any war the horse is led through a triple fence of crossed lances — right foot first means victory, and the wrong step forbids the expedition.
summary.zh: 斯萬托維特畜神聖白馬，由大祭司親飼，晨起見汗——神於夜間乘之征戰；凡有戰事，牽馬越三重交矛之柵：右足先跨則勝，錯步則罷兵。

passages.text: A beautiful white horse was consecrated to Svantovit, fed and groomed by the head priest, whom the Rugians honoured as they would the king. The people believed that Svantovit, mounted on this steed, fought by night against those who opposed his worship; in the morning the horse was often found bathed in sweat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 1, after Saxo; not verbatim.

passages.text: Success or failure in weighty enterprises was divined by the animal. Before a warlike expedition the priests erected three rows of palings, each of two lances driven into the ground with a third laid across them; after solemn prayer the priest led the sacred horse to the palings. If it stepped over right foot first the omen was favourable; if the order was reversed, the expedition had to be abandoned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 1; not verbatim.

title.en: The Fall of Arkona, 1168: The Demon Leaves the Broken God
title.zh: 一一六八年阿科納陷落：魔影自碎神而出

region.en: Arkona, isle of Rugen (symbolic pin at Cape Arkona)
region.zh: 呂根島阿科納（象徵性定位於阿科納角）

texts.period: Event of 1168; recorded by Saxo Grammaticus c. 1200 (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 1, after Saxo Grammaticus

summary.en: When King Valdemar of Denmark took Arkona in 1168 the Rugians stood expecting Svantovit to annihilate the enemy to the last; instead the idol was roped and dragged down, a black animal was seen to flee from it, and the god of the western Slavs was smashed and burned.
summary.zh: 一一六八年丹麥王瓦爾德馬攻陷阿科納，呂根人直至最後猶信斯萬托維特將殲敵；神像終遭繩索拖倒，黑獸竄逸，西斯拉夫大神碎而焚之。

sensitivity.note: Historical conquest narrative from the conquerors' side; recorded as such.

passages.text: In 1168 Valdemar, king of the Danes, conquered Arkona after strong resistance. He first seized the treasure of the temple and then ordered the destruction of the sanctuary. A vast multitude of the inhabitants assembled, expecting every moment that Svantovit would annihilate their enemies; but the statue itself was finally torn down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 1, after Saxo; not verbatim.

passages.text: The demon was said to have left the idol in the shape of a black animal which disappeared before the eyes of the spectators. The Danes cast ropes around the god and dragged him to the ground in sight of the Slavs; smashed in pieces, he was burned. The treasure — the offerings of tribute-paying nations, the tithes of war and freebooting gathered by three hundred horsemen devoted to the god — passed to the conquerors, and with it the independence of the western Slavs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 1; not verbatim.

title.en: Triglav of Stettin: The Three-Headed God with the Veiled Face
title.zh: 斯德丁的三頭神：蒙面之特里格拉夫

region.zh: 波美拉尼亞斯德丁（什切青）

texts.period: Recorded by Ebbo/Otto of Bamberg's biographers, early 12th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 2

summary.en: On the central hill of Stettin stood the golden idol of Triglav, three-headed because he rules heaven, earth, and the underworld, veiled because he will not see the sins of men; his black horse, led thrice over nine lances, gave oracles for war — until Bishop Otto broke the statue and sent its head to the Pope.
summary.zh: 斯德丁中央山丘立特里格拉夫金像：三首以示其治天、地、冥三界，蒙面以示不視人罪；黑馬三越九矛以卜戰事——主教奧托碎其像，獻首於教皇。

passages.text: In the town of Stettin were three hills, the central one dedicated to Triglav, the chief local deity. His idol was of gold with three heads, its eyes and lips covered with a golden veil. The pagan priests declared that Triglav — 'Three-Heads' — was tricephalous because he ruled over three realms, heaven, earth, and the underworld, and that he covered his face because he would not see the sins of men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 2; not verbatim.

passages.text: The chief of Stettin's four temples was built with wonderful skill, its inner and outer walls covered with embossed figures of men, birds, and animals that seemed to live and breathe. A tenth of all booty was stored in its treasury, with golden horns of wild bulls, gilded and jewelled, some for drinking, some for sounding. A black horse of noble stature was kept for the god: led thrice across nine lances planted before the temple, if he stepped over without touching any, the warlike expedition was decided upon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 2; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Bishop Otto of Bamberg destroyed the heathen temples, the Slav priests of Wollin are said to have carried their Triglav secretly to a lonely woman, who hid it in the hollow of a large tree; a German, pretending to thank the god for saving him from shipwreck, betrayed her and stole the idol's old saddle. Otto himself broke the Stettin statue and sent its head to the Pope; churches of St. Ethelbert and St. Peter rose on the hill once sacred to Triglav.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 2; not verbatim.

title.en: Svarazic of Radgost: The Son of Svarog Armed in Bison and Bird
title.zh: 拉迪戈斯特的斯瓦拉日茨：佩野牛紋、戴鳥盔之神子

region.en: Radgost (Rethra), land of the Lutices between Elbe and Oder
region.zh: 盧蒂奇人之地拉迪戈斯特（雷特拉）

texts.period: Recorded by Thietmar (c. 1012) and Adam of Bremen (c. 1075); recorded by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 3, after Thietmar and Adam of Bremen

summary.en: In the wooden temple of Radgost the Rhetarii kept Svarazic, 'Son of Svarog', in golden armour, his helmet shaped like a bird with outstretched wings and the black bison of the tribe on his breast; all the Slavic nations came to his oracles — and in 1066 the head of a captured bishop was offered at his altar.
summary.zh: 拉迪戈斯特木構神廟中，雷塔里人奉斯瓦拉日茨——『斯瓦羅格之子』——著金甲、戴展翅鳥盔、胸前飾部族黑野牛紋；斯拉夫諸族皆來求神諭——一〇六六年，被俘主教之首祭於其壇。

sensitivity.note: Historical chronicle material including a recorded human sacrifice; described critically, not endorsed.

passages.text: The Rhetarii, a division of the Lutices between the Elbe and the Oder, worshipped Svarazic — 'Son of Svarog'. The chronicler Thietmar testifies that their castle of Radigast contained a wooden temple full of statues of divinities, made by human hands, wearing armour and helmets that struck terror into beholders, each with his name carved on his image. St. Bruno, apostle of the Prussians, writing to Emperor Henry II, calls him 'Zuarasiz diabolus' — Svarazic the devil.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 3, after Thietmar and Adam of Bremen; not verbatim.

passages.text: Adam of Bremen describes the god in a spacious sanctuary among other deities: made of gold, his base adorned with brocade, his helmet resembling a bird with outstretched wings, the head of a black bison — emblem of the Rhetarii — on his breast, his right hand resting on it and his left grasping a double-edged axe. The temple was visited by all the Slavic nations for prophecy and the annual festivities; and in 1066, in honour of a victory, the head of John, bishop of Mecklenburg, taken in battle, was offered up to this divinity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 3; not verbatim.

title.en: Cernobog: The Toast to the Black God
title.zh: 切爾諾博格：敬黑神之酒

region.en: Elbe Slavic lands (symbolic pin at Lubeck)
region.zh: 易北斯拉夫人之地（象徵性定位於呂貝克）

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 4, after Helmold

summary.en: At their feasts the Elbe Slavs passed a cup around and uttered words in honour of the gods of good and evil alike, believing happiness from the good god but all misfortune from Cernobog, the Black God — and asking the Black God to be merciful.
summary.zh: 易北斯拉夫人宴席上傳杯致祭善惡二神：謂幸福出自善神，一切不幸皆由黑神切爾諾博格所降——故亦求黑神垂憐。

sensitivity.note: The dual-god formula parallels Zoroastrian dualism and Chernobog's modern pop-culture fame; interpretive tagging.

passages.text: Helmold records that at banquets the Slavs were wont to offer prayers to a divinity of good and one of evil: convinced that happiness comes from the god of good and misfortune from the deity of evil, they called the latter Cernobog, the 'Black God'. When the cup went round they uttered words — not only of praise, it seemed, but of appeasement toward the Black God as well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 4, after Helmold; not verbatim.

passages.text: Machal reads the figure critically: the conception of Cernobog as the god of evil probably reflects Christian influence, the western Slavs having transferred to a devil-figure traits of the old deities. He was regarded as the cause of all calamities, and the prayers at banquets were in reality meant to avert misfortune. His bright counterpart, Byelobog the 'White God', appears only in late folk tradition.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 4; not verbatim.

title.en: Ziva: The Goddess of the Living

region.en: Polabian lands between Elbe and Baltic (symbolic pin at Lubeck)
region.zh: 易北河至波羅的海之間的波拉比亞（象徵性定位於呂貝克）

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 5

summary.en: The Elbe Slavs worshipped goddesses as well as gods; the only female divinity whose name survives is Ziva, 'the Living', goddess of the Polabians — while the Lutices once angrily avenged an affront done to a goddess whose name is lost.
summary.zh: 易北斯拉夫人既祀男神亦祀女神；女性神祇中唯其名傳世者為日瓦——『生者』，波拉比亞人之女神；盧蒂奇人曾為某失名女神受辱而憤然復仇。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary source; interpretive reconstruction flagged in note.

passages.text: Besides the great male deities the Elbe Slavs worshipped goddesses. Thietmar states that the walls of the temples of Radgost were adorned with figures of deities both male and female, and elsewhere tells how the Lutices angrily resented an affront done to a goddess. The only female divinity actually named, however, is Siva — Ziva, 'the Living' — whom Helmold calls goddess of the Polabians; her Polish counterpart is the Zywie of old tradition.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 5; not verbatim.

passages.text: Other names drift through the sources without stories: Pripegala, likened by an astonished archbishop to Priapus; Podaga of Helmold's list; Turupid, Pisamar, and Tiernoglav from the Knytlingasaga. Whatever their rites, the memory of the Baltic-Slav pantheon died with the conversion of the twelfth century — only the bare names and this one goddess of life remain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 5; not verbatim.

title.en: The Gods of Korenice: Seven Faces, Five Heads, and the Forbidden Shield
title.zh: 科倫尼察諸神：七面五首與禁觸之盾

region.en: Isle of Rugen and Wolgast, Baltic coast
region.zh: 呂根島與沃爾加斯特，波羅的海沿岸

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 5

summary.en: Around Arkona stood the sister-shrines: Rugievit, an oak colossus with seven faces and eight swords; Porevit with five heads; Porenutius with four faces and a fifth in his breast; and at Wolgast, Gerovit, war-god of the golden shield that no mortal hand might touch in time of peace.
summary.zh: 阿科納周邊眾姊妹神廟：魯吉耶維特，橡木巨人七面八劍；波列維特五首；波列努提烏斯四面、胸前復一面；沃爾加斯特有戰神蓋羅維特，其金盾非戰時凡人之手不可觸。

passages.text: In the sanctuary of Korenice (modern Garz) on Rugen stood a colossal oaken idol called Rugievit, so high that Bishop Absalon, though a very tall man, could scarcely reach its chin with his axe as he broke it. The image had a single head with seven faces, seven swords hung in its belt, and an eighth blade in its hand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 5, after Saxo; not verbatim.

passages.text: Another sanctuary held Porevit, five-headed and unarmed, and Porenutius, whose idol had four faces with a fifth in its breast, the left hand raised to its forehead and the right touching its chin. The Pomeranians of Wolgast worshipped Gerovit, a war-god whose enormous shield, wrought with gold, hung in his shrine: carried before the army it ensured victory, but it could be taken down only in time of war, and mortal hands were forbidden to touch it. All these idols appear as local analogues of Svantovit himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part II ch. 5; not verbatim.
